sources.citation: Grimes, Charles E. & Owen Edwards. 2026. The Austronesian languages of eastern Indonesia and Timor-Leste: Unravelling their prehistory and classification. Berlin: Language Science Press. Section 11.4 'Teor-Kur', pp. 464-468 (open access, Zenodo 18323007).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing. Section 11.4 is historical phonology (sound correspondences) only, and states p. 464: 'Data is extremely scarce for both languages.. the only accessible data for Teor is the word list in Wallace (1869). The only data for Kur we have been able to access is the word list in von Rosenberg (1867: 108-114), as well as two folktales, Ohoiwutun (2021) and Rado (2021)'; fn. 12 mentions a 479-item Teor wordlist from Craig Marshall received at press time, not reproduced. No stress marks in any Teor/Kur form cited.

sources.citation: Hughes, Jock. 1987. The languages of Kei, Tanimbar and Aru: a lexicostatistic classification. NUSA (Linguistic Studies of Indonesian and Other Languages in Indonesia) 27: 71-111. Section 2.1.2.2 'Teor-Kur', p. 84.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing. Image-only scan, scanned (tesseract, 100 dpi render of 300 ppi CCITT pages). Only phonetic remark (p. 84): 'There are some consistent phonetic changes between Kur and Ut, particularly the palatalisation in Ut of word-final alveolar nasals, laterals and voiceless alveolar plosives in Kur. Also, velar nasals in Kur become voiced velar plosives in Ut.' No stress/accent anywhere in the 41 pages.

sources.citation: Collins, James T. 1982. Linguistic Research in Maluku: A Report of Recent Field Work. Oceanic Linguistics 21(1/2): 73-146, esp. pp. 122-123 (Teor-Kur).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: a digital copy exists, behind a library sign-in (also a publisher record (DOI), probably paywalled)
sources.note: Only professional linguist's first-hand field report on Teor-Kur before 1987; Collins routinely notes stress in his Maluku sketches, so pp. 122-123 (and any Teor-Kur wordlist appendix) are the single most likely place for a one-line stress remark.

sources.citation: Wallace, Alfred R. 1869. The Malay Archipelago, vol. 2. London: Macmillan. Appendix 'One hundred and seventeen words in thirty-three languages', language no. 46 Teor (archive.org malayarchipelago02wall).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No rule. General note to the vocabularies: 'Long, short, and accented syllables are marked in the usual way.' Teor forms carry per-word acute accents (as re-transcribed by Grimes & Edwards: ‹rúa› 'two', ‹hutá› 'ten', ‹meránna›, ‹fudarúa›), i.e. raw accent data on ~117 words, mixed positions; the archive.org scanned drops most diacritics so no census was attempted.

sources.citation: von Rosenberg, C. B. H. 1867. Reis naar de zuidoostereilanden, gedaan in 1865. 's Gravenhage: Martinus Nijhoff. 'Vergelijkende woordenlijst' with Koor (Kur) and 'Tijoor' columns, pp. 107 ff. (archive.org reis-naar-de-zuidoostereilanden).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Pronunciation note p. 107 only: French accents on e for vowel quality, breve/macron for short vs long syllables. (Grimes & Edwards 2026 fn. 13: the 'Tijoor' list is actually a Geser-Gorom variety; only the Koor list is Teor-Kur.)
